headline: U.S. votes in midterms as oil falls on Iran talks hopes
briefing: Americans vote today in midterm elections that will decide control of Congress, with markets watching for effects on trade and the Iran conflict. Oil fell about 6% on Monday on hopes for U.S.-Iran talks, though reports conflict on further strikes. In Ottawa, the federal budget arrives Thursday amid warnings that deficits are deepening.

stories.backstory: The U.S. and Israel began striking Iran on Feb. 28, and Iran responded by choking traffic through the Strait of Hormuz, the route for about a fifth of the world's oil. A June peace memorandum briefly reopened the strait, but it collapsed in July and the U.S. imposed a blockade on Iranian shipping. Yemen's Houthis have since widened the fight with missile attacks on Saudi Arabia, and Egypt's parliament has authorized sending troops to help the Saudis. Qatar handed Iran a new draft deal on Oct. 25, which Tehran said contained ideas it could not accept.
stories.headline: Oil drops on U.S.-Iran diplomacy hopes as midterm vote arrives
stories.impact: Expect GTA gas and diesel prices to stay high, which feeds into grocery, delivery and transit costs. Alberta oil revenues rise, but Ontario households and manufacturers mostly feel the cost side.
stories.now: Brent crude fell about 6% on Monday to roughly US$106 a barrel during the session, after ending October at US$113.43, as traders bet on a diplomatic opening; those figures are intraday, not closing prices. Secretary of State Marco Rubio reportedly said Trump has not decided to attack Iran, and earlier reports said Trump would hold off on strikes until after the midterms, but one report later said the U.S. hit Qeshm Island, so the picture is unclear. Qatari mediators have a plan to reopen the Strait of Hormuz, and Iran says its conditions include lifting sanctions and guarantees against new attacks. No signed deal or restored shipping access has been confirmed.

stories.headline: Ottawa tables federal budget Thursday as deficit worries mount
stories.summary: Finance Minister François-Philippe Champagne will table the budget on Nov. 5, with the Parliamentary Budget Officer warning deficits are deepening.
stories.now: Champagne has set Thursday, Nov. 5 for the second budget since the Liberals moved it to the fall. The Parliamentary Budget Officer (PBO), Parliament's independent fiscal watchdog, projects this year's shortfall at $65.3 billion and says the deficit will still be above $63 billion in 2030-31, versus the $53 billion Ottawa projected in April. The budget is likely to be judged on whether it lays out a deficit path the PBO can verify. The Bank of Canada's policy rate stands at 2.50%.
stories.backstory: The Carney government shifted the federal budget from spring to fall last year. Its first fall budget, on Nov. 4, 2025, projected a $78.3 billion deficit for that year, the largest outside the pandemic years. Since then the government has pushed spending restraint while also promising large investments, and trade tension with the U.S. has weighed on growth.
stories.why: The budget sets federal spending, taxes and borrowing, and shows how Ottawa plans to respond to trade pressure and slower growth. Larger deficits can also affect interest rates and the government's room for future programs.
stories.impact: Ontario households could see changes to taxes, benefits, housing and infrastructure spending, including transit and trade-affected industries. Watch for measures aimed at auto and manufacturing workers in the GTA.
